sa_market_summary: The Isuzu D-Max is the third best-selling bakkie in South Africa behind the Toyota Hilux and Ford Ranger, but earns a reputation as the most reliable and durable of the three. The 7th generation (2022+) is built locally at Isuzu's Struandale plant in Gqeberha. It offers two diesel engines: the 1.9 DDi (110kW/350Nm) and the legendary 3.0 DDi (140kW/450Nm), both known for linear power delivery and exceptional longevity. The D-Max is the preferred choice for farmers and fleet operators who plan to keep their vehicles past 300,000km. Isuzu's 5-year/120,000km warranty and 6-year/90,000km service plan add peace of mind. Resale value is strong though slightly below the Hilux.

known_faults.description: Like all modern diesels with DPF systems, the D-Max's diesel particulate filter can clog if the vehicle is used mainly for short city trips where regeneration cannot complete. The 1.9 DDi is more sensitive than the 3.0 DDi.
known_faults.what_to_inspect: Ask about driving patterns — frequent highway driving is beneficial. Check for a DPF warning light. Request DPF regeneration history.
known_faults.estimated_repair_zar: R3,000 - R15,000 (forced regeneration to DPF replacement)
known_faults.source: Isuzu SA dealer bulletins, SA bakkie owner forums

known_faults.description: The common-rail injection system is sensitive to contaminated or poor-quality diesel. Dirty fuel can lead to injector failure, which is an expensive repair common to all modern turbodiesels.
known_faults.what_to_inspect: Verify that the owner fills up at reputable stations. Request service records showing fuel filter changes. Check for any injector-related fault codes.
known_faults.source: Isuzu SA technical bulletins, SA diesel specialist workshops

known_faults.description: Fleet and work-use D-Maxes show accelerated suspension wear — rear leaf spring fatigue, worn control arm bushes, and steering play are common on vehicles that have been regularly loaded to capacity.
known_faults.what_to_inspect: Check rear leaf springs for sagging or cracked leaves. Test steering for play. Listen for suspension clunks over speed bumps.
known_faults.source: Isuzu SA workshop data, SA 4x4 community reports

known_faults.description: The 9-inch infotainment system can intermittently refuse USB inputs while driving, forcing reliance on Bluetooth streaming. Software updates have addressed some cases.
known_faults.what_to_inspect: Test USB connectivity with your own phone. Check that Apple CarPlay/Android Auto connects reliably.
known_faults.estimated_repair_zar: R0 (software update) to R5,000 (head unit replacement)
known_faults.source: Isuzu SA owner reports, TechBrunch SA review

what_to_inspect_before_buying: Request full Isuzu dealer service history — critical for warranty validity
Check underbody condition — look for rust, damage, and evidence of off-road abuse
Verify DPF system has been properly maintained if used mostly for short trips
Test 4WD system (if equipped) — engage high and low range, check for warning lights
Check for any injector-related fault codes via diagnostic scan
Inspect leaf springs for sagging or cracked leaves
Verify outstanding recall completion (Takata airbag, software updates)
Check the 1.9 DDi's timing belt replacement history (every 120,000km)
owner_sentiment: Strongly positive. D-Max owners are among the most loyal in the bakkie segment. The 3.0 DDi engine is revered for its bulletproof reliability and linear power delivery. The 1.9 DDi is more fuel-efficient but less punchy. Main complaints are the dated interior design compared to the newer Ranger, occasional infotainment glitches, and firm ride quality (though better than previous generations). Resale value is strong but trails the Hilux. Isuzu's dealer network is well-regarded for aftersales service.
